in_context.text: Paul has just told the men to pray without wrath and doubting (2:8). "In like manner" he now turns to the women. He asks them to be marked by modesty, self-control, and good works rather than costly display (2:9-10).

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself at the start of the letter. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote in his name.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul had left to lead the church at Ephesus. Through him the instruction reaches the church.

affected.text: The women of the church, especially as believers gathered for prayer and worship.

what.text: Women are to adorn themselves with orderly, modest clothing, a sense of shame, and self-control. They should not rely on braided hair, gold, pearls, or very expensive clothing. Their true adornment should be good works, which fits women who profess godliness.

events.text: The verse does not describe a single event. It gives standing instructions for how the church should conduct itself in worship.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, by Paul, between his Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110 and see it as written in Paul's name, though others defend the earlier date and Paul's authorship.

where.text: The instruction is for the church at Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia.

purpose.text: Paul wants the church's worship to reflect godliness. Just as men are to pray without wrath, women are to show modesty and good works rather than displays of wealth.

big_picture.text: A key theme of the letter is that sound teaching produces godly living, so belief and behavior go together. Peter gives a similar teaching, putting inner character above outward adornment.

for_readers.text: The verse asks readers to consider what they put on display. The point is not mainly clothing but whether a person's life is "adorned" with self-control and good works.

misuse.popular_reading: Quoted as a universal dress code that forbids all braids, jewelry, or makeup, or as a rule mainly about covering the body.

in_context_reading.text: The contrast in the passage is between costly display and good works (2:9-10). The words used point to very expensive, sumptuous attire in a wealthy city. The verse does not mention makeup, and its stress falls on modest, self-controlled character.

why_it_matters.text: The verb's root meaning is to order or arrange. Paul is not forbidding adornment. He redirects it toward modesty and good works.
This rare word can mean a garment, but it can also mean steadiness or quietness of demeanour. So it may point to bearing and behavior, not only clothing.
In older English "shamefacedness" did not mean embarrassment. The Greek means a sense of shame or modesty, a fitting reserve.
The word means soundness of mind and self-control, not abstaining from alcohol. It appears again in 2:15.
The word means very costly or of great value. This shows the target is extravagant display of wealth, not ordinary clothing.

takeaway.text: Paul asks women to be marked by modesty and self-control, and by good works rather than displays of wealth.
